title: Streaming generation internals — chunking, flush policy, cancellation, partial tokens
content:
Status: draft — working spec for streaming generation flush / chunking / cancellation semantics and interactions with KV cache and kernel scheduling.

Context and goals:
- This is a runtime-level spec describing how we emit partial/generated output to clients (hosted API and Dedicated/private proxies) and how that interacts with batching, KV cache, and kernel preemption.
- Primary goals: predictable latency for first-byte and subsequent bytes, bounded memory for partial outputs, correct semantics under cancellation and resends, and minimal wasted GPU work on canceled requests.
- Secondary goals: make behaviour simple enough for SDKs to reason about (replay, resume), and make metrics actionable (time-to-first-chunk, tokens-per-chunk, flush-rate).

Assumptions and constraints:
- We treat model inference as a sequence-of-steps producing tokens (or subtoken logits). The kernel executes step N => step N+1 atomic unit; kernels cannot be interrupted mid-step without doing extra bookkeeping.
- Batching: multiple requests may be coalesced into a batch. The flush policy must play nicely with batching; a single request should not block flush for the whole batch.
- KV cache: model context uses KV cache per request. Cache entries are append-only for a generation session; caching must remain consistent even for canceled requests (see below).
- Network: clients expect streaming chunks (server-sent events / HTTP chunked / WebSocket). SDKs may optionally buffer partial chunks until token boundaries.

Key definitions:
- micro-chunk: small unit we emit frequently (e.g., 1–4 tokens). Tunable per model.
- macro-chunk: group of micro-chunks aggregated to reduce network overhead (e.g., 8–32 tokens).
- flush: action of sending currently buffered micro-chunks for a request to the client.
- partial token: bytes that represent an incomplete UTF-8/grapheme sequence for a tokenized token when detokenization happens incrementally.
- tombstone/canceled: marked state for requests that were canceled or timed out; may still be in-flight in kernel / batch.

Chunking policy (recommended default):
- Emit micro-chunks at token boundaries whenever available. Default micro-chunk size: 1 token.
- Aggregate up to macro-chunk size (default 8 tokens) or max latency per flush (default 50ms), whichever comes first.
- If a request is generating slowly (e.g., model stalls), emit whatever is available after the max-latency timer. This ensures bounded time-to-first-byte behavior.
- For high-throughput modes (batch-heavy, low-latency SLOs), allow larger macro-chunk sizes (16–32 tokens) configurable per route.
- Edge case: when micro-chunk tokenization produces large unicode grapheme clusters newlines etc., treat detokenized char-length ceiling (e.g., 1024 bytes) to avoid sending multi-megabyte chunk in single flush.

Flush policy (interaction with batching):
- Each request tracks its own flush buffer. The batch scheduler should call kernel.step() for the batch, and when the step produces output for N requests, the runtime updates each request's buffer.
- A per-request flush timer (50ms default) is started when the first micro-token is appended to an empty buffer. If more tokens arrive before timeout, aggregate until either macro-chunk size or timeout.
- Cross-request flush coalescing: to reduce syscalls, if multiple requests within a batch are ready to flush within 5ms, we coalesce writes to the same connection. This is an optimization and must not change logical per-request ordering.
- Immediate flush triggers: final token (EOS), explicit flush API from SDK (e.g., flush now), or backpressure from client (e.g., window zero).

Partial tokens and detokenizer behavior:
- We must distinguish two streaming models: token-level streaming and byte/grapheme streaming. For consistency across models and tokenizer families, default to token-level streaming: emit completed tokens only.
- When the detokenizer can produce partial UTF-8 output (e.g., BPE splits that map to unicode bytes incrementally), we do not emit raw partial bytes by default. Instead:
  - Strategy A (default): hold until token detokenization completes for the token, then emit. This avoids broken unicode sequences.
  - Strategy B (opt-in): allow byte-level streaming for ultra-low-latency paths (experimental), but tag events as partial=true and provide sequence_offset so SDKs can assemble safely. Only allowed on routes that opt in and where client agrees to handle correction/edits.
- For languages with complex script (emoji, CJK), prefer Strategy A to avoid user-visible glitches.

Cancellation and preemption semantics:
- API-level cancel: client sends cancel request -> runtime marks request as tombstoned and returns 202-accepted for cancel.
- If request is in batch and kernel has not started the step that will produce new tokens, we may remove it from the batch for the next step to avoid scheduling wasted work. If kernel is mid-step for that request, we cannot interrupt the kernel; we must finish the step, but we should avoid scheduling further steps for that request.
- If request has pending buffered tokens (not yet flushed), we should flush them on cancellation unless the client specified drop_on_cancel=true. Default: flush buffered tokens (best-effort) then emit cancellation marker (stream end with cancellation flag).
- For GPU cost accounting: canceled requests that finish mid-step still count as work performed. We should tag metrics accordingly (cancelled_after_work = true).
- For KV cache: do not commit generation progress to durable shared caches on cancellation unless the request completed an explicit commit hook. In other words, KV cache remains per-session in memory; only persisted variants (e.g., prefix caching for future reuse) are written when full generation completes. This avoids polluting the cache with partial/incorrect states.

Replay / resume semantics:
- Resume support requires that the client replays previous tokens and the server reinstates a session with equivalent KV cache. Because we do not persist partial KV cache on cancel by default, resumption is only supported if the client provides explicit context (previous tokens) or if the route opts into partial-commit semantics.
- Suggestion: implement a resume token (session snapshot id) for dedicated/private customers that want resume semantics. This is a separate feature (INF-xxxx).

Scheduling & kernel implications:
- Kernel step is atomic; cancellation cannot stop the kernel mid-step without complex preemption support. We therefore:
  - Prioritize scheduling so that short/latency-critical requests are placed in high-preempt queues (fast-path) with smaller batch windows.
  - Long-running/background jobs use lower-priority queues with larger batch windows to increase throughput.
- For preemption we support two approaches (hybrid):
  1) cooperative preemption: kernels yield at defined checkpoints (e.g., after token generation and before KV append) — cheapest to implement.
  2) hardware-assisted preemption: if GPU supports ECC / MPS-like isolation, implement true preemptible kernels — more complex/hardware dependent.
- We must expose scheduling knobs per route: max_wait_for_batch_ms, max_macro_chunk_tokens, priority_class. These are part of route config and should be surfaced in Console.

KV cache interaction notes:
- KV entries are appended as tokens are generated; we keep per-session in-memory KV cache until session termination.
- For batching: each request has private KV pointers; batching simply mixes kernel inputs but KV appends are per-request.
- For canceled requests: do not expose partial KV cache to other sessions. If we decide to persist, mark entries as provisional and GC after TTL if not committed.
- Memory management: aggressively free KV cache for tombstoned/cancelled sessions after a short grace period (default 1s) unless a resume token is requested. This avoids memory blowups from many aborted sessions.

API / SDK implications:
- Clients should expect token-level streaming by default and not rely on partial-byte streaming unless route explicitly supports it.
- Cancellation is best-effort; clients should be prepared to receive a small number of additional tokens after cancel acknowledgment. SDK will expose cancel() that returns a promise resolving when server emits final cancellation event (or timeout).
- New SDK flags: dropOnCancel (bool), byteLevelStreaming (bool), resumeToken (string).

Metrics and observability:
- Emit the following per-request metrics: time_to_first_chunk_ms, avg_tokens_per_chunk, flush_rate_per_sec, canceled_after_kernel_step, bytes_sent_partial, kv_cache_bytes, resume_token_issued.
- Add traces for: flush_timer_start, flush_timer_fire, cancel_received, cancel_flushed, kernel_step_start/finish per-request.

Backwards compatibility and rollout plan:
- Default behavior keeps token-level streaming and flush timer 50ms, macro-chunk 8 tokens.
- Flag-gated features: byte-level streaming and partial-commit KV. Begin rollout internal-only for Dedicated preview customers.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we provide an option to persist provisional KV entries for resumption use-cases? If yes, what are privacy/consent implications? (security asked to weigh in)
- Exact default timers need benchmarking across models and hardware. TODO: run perf matrix for 7B/13B/70B models across T4/A10/A100 and gather time-to-first-byte and cost curves (INF-3421).
- Handler for client backpressure over slow connections: how long do we buffer before dropping tokens? Proposal: per-connection buffer cap 1MB or 20 tokens per request; beyond that, stop producing further tokens (apply backpressure to scheduler). Need design for backpressure propagation into scheduler.
- How to handle mixed-token and byte-level streaming for multimodal outputs (e.g., attachments, images outbound)? Separate path?

Quick implementation notes and pointers:
- Runtime changes: streaming_buffer per request; flush_timer engine; cancellation state machine; per-route knobs in route config; metrics instrumentation points.
- Code pointers: serving-runtime/streaming/flush_manager.go, serving-runtime/scheduler/batcher.go, serving-runtime/kv/cache_manager.go (draft branches in PR #1217).
- Tests to add: correctness on cancel during batch, partial token safety for emoji/CJK, perf benchmarks for various chunk sizes, and resume/commit flows.

Appendix: example event sequence
- t0: client POST /generate -> server assigns session id S1, starts kernel queue.
- t0+70ms: kernel returns first token tkn1 -> runtime buffers tkn1, starts per-request flush timer.
- t0+100ms: more tokens arrive tkn2..tkn4 -> macro-chunk hits 4 tokens but below macro limit, wait for timer.
- t0+120ms: timer fires (max 50ms) -> runtime flushes tokens tkn1..tkn4 to client in single chunk.
- t0+121ms: client sends cancel() -> runtime marks S1 tombstoned; there are 2 tokens in-flight in batch; once kernel finishes step, runtime flushes remaining tokens then sends cancellation final event.

Notes to reviewers: please comment on the cancellation flush behaviour (default flush-on-cancel vs drop-on-cancel) and whether the resume-token approach is acceptable for Dedicated customers who need resume semantics.

Signed-off-by: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
